import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Bipartite graphs: do crown graphs require the longest word-representants?

A graph $G = (V, E)$ is *word-representable* if there is a word $w$ over the alphabet $V$ (every
letter of $V$ occurring in $w$) such that two distinct letters $x, y$ *alternate* in $w$ if and
only if $xy \in E$. Here $x$ and $y$ alternate in $w$ if deleting from $w$ all letters other than
$x$ and $y$ leaves a word of the form $xyxy\cdots$ or $yxyx\cdots$ (of even or odd length). The
graph $G$ is *$k$-representable* if it is represented by a word containing exactly $k$ copies of
each letter; the least such $k$ is the *representation number* $\mathcal{R}(G)$. A word
representing a graph on $n$ vertices with $k$ copies of each letter has length $kn$, so
$\mathcal{R}(G)$ measures the length of the shortest uniform word-representant of $G$. Every
bipartite graph is word-representable.

The *crown graph* $H_{m,m}$ is obtained from the complete bipartite graph $K_{m,m}$ by removing a
perfect matching. Glen, Kitaev and Pyatkin proved that $\mathcal{R}(H_{m,m}) = \lceil m/2 \rceil$
for $m \ge 5$.

The open problem asks whether, among all bipartite graphs, the crown graphs require the longest
word-representants: is $\mathcal{R}(G) \le \mathcal{R}(H_{m,m})$ for every bipartite graph $G$
on $2m$ vertices?

*References:*
- [Wikipedia, Bipartite graph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/bipartite_graph)
- [Wikipedia, List of unsolved problems in mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_unsolved_problems_in_mathematics)
- S. Kitaev, *A comprehensive introduction to the theory of word-representable graphs*,
  [arXiv:1705.05924](https://arxiv.org/abs/1705.05924)
- M. Glen, S. Kitaev, A. Pyatkin, *On the representation number of a crown graph*,
  Discrete Applied Mathematics 244 (2018), 89–93,
  [arXiv:1609.00674](https://arxiv.org/abs/1609.00674)
- S. Kitaev, V. Lozin, *Words and Graphs*, Monographs in Theoretical Computer Science,
  Springer (2015)
-/
namespace BipartiteGraph
open SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [DecidableEq V]

blocks.code:
def Alternate (w : List V) (x y : V) : Prop :=
  (w.filter fun z => z = x ∨ z = y).IsChain (· ≠ ·)
blocks.docstring:
Two letters `x` and `y` *alternate* in the word `w` if deleting from `w` all letters other
than `x` and `y` leaves a word with no two consecutive equal letters, i.e. a word of the form
`xyxy…` or `yxyx…` (of even or odd length).

justification.closest_existing_considered: List.IsChain / List.Pairwise / List.Sublist; none expresses alternation of two letters in a word, so a one-line wrapper was needed.
justification.name: BipartiteGraph.Alternate
justification.why_needed: Core notion of the word-representable-graph literature: letters x, y alternate in w if the subword of w on {x, y} has no two consecutive equal letters (i.e. is xyxy… or yxyx…). Encoded as `(w.filter fun z => z = x ∨ z = y).IsChain (· ≠ ·)`.

blocks.name: Alternate
blocks.text:
/-- Two letters `x` and `y` *alternate* in the word `w` if deleting from `w` all letters other
than `x` and `y` leaves a word with no two consecutive equal letters, i.e. a word of the form
`xyxy…` or `yxyx…` (of even or odd length). -/
def Alternate (w : List V) (x y : V) : Prop :=
  (w.filter fun z => z = x ∨ z = y).IsChain (· ≠ ·)

blocks.code:
def IsRepresentedBy (G : SimpleGraph V) (w : List V) : Prop :=
  (∀ v, v ∈ w) ∧ ∀ x y, x ≠ y → (Alternate w x y ↔ G.Adj x y)
blocks.docstring:
A word `w` over the alphabet `V` *represents* the graph `G` if every letter of `V` occurs in
`w`, and two distinct letters alternate in `w` if and only if they are adjacent in `G`.

justification.closest_existing_considered: No Mathlib or repo counterpart (searched for word-represent / semi-transitive / alternat in Mathlib and FormalConjectures*).
justification.name: BipartiteGraph.IsRepresentedBy
justification.why_needed: A word w over alphabet V represents G: every letter of V occurs in w and, for distinct x y, `Alternate w x y ↔ G.Adj x y`. Nothing in Mathlib models word-representable graphs.

blocks.name: IsRepresentedBy
blocks.text:
/-- A word `w` over the alphabet `V` *represents* the graph `G` if every letter of `V` occurs in
`w`, and two distinct letters alternate in `w` if and only if they are adjacent in `G`. -/
def IsRepresentedBy (G : SimpleGraph V) (w : List V) : Prop :=
  (∀ v, v ∈ w) ∧ ∀ x y, x ≠ y → (Alternate w x y ↔ G.Adj x y)

blocks.code:
def IsKRepresentable (G : SimpleGraph V) (k : ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∃ w : List V, IsRepresentedBy G w ∧ ∀ v, w.count v = k
blocks.docstring:
The graph `G` is *`k`-representable* if it is represented by a word containing exactly `k`
copies of each letter.

justification.name: BipartiteGraph.IsKRepresentable
justification.why_needed: G is k-representable if some representing word has exactly k copies (`List.count`) of every letter; needed to define the representation number.

blocks.name: IsKRepresentable
blocks.text:
/-- The graph `G` is *`k`-representable* if it is represented by a word containing exactly `k`
copies of each letter. -/
def IsKRepresentable (G : SimpleGraph V) (k : ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∃ w : List V, IsRepresentedBy G w ∧ ∀ v, w.count v = k

blocks.code:
noncomputable def representationNumber (G : SimpleGraph V) : ℕ :=
  sInf {k | IsKRepresentable G k}
blocks.docstring:
The *representation number* $\mathcal{R}(G)$ of `G`: the least `k` such that `G` is
`k`-representable. By the `sInf` convention it is `0` when `G` is not word-representable; this
does not occur for bipartite graphs, which are all word-representable.

justification.closest_existing_considered: Other sInf-style graph invariants in FormalConjecturesForMathlib (dominationNumber, pathCoverNumber) as style models; no existing invariant matches.
justification.name: BipartiteGraph.representationNumber
justification.why_needed: The representation number R(G) = sInf {k | G is k-representable}, the invariant the problem compares. Verified by the API lemma `representationNumber_top` (complete graphs have R = 1, as in the literature).

blocks.name: representationNumber
blocks.text:
/-- The *representation number* $\mathcal{R}(G)$ of `G`: the least `k` such that `G` is
`k`-representable. By the `sInf` convention it is `0` when `G` is not word-representable; this
does not occur for bipartite graphs, which are all word-representable. -/
noncomputable def representationNumber (G : SimpleGraph V) : ℕ :=
  sInf {k | IsKRepresentable G k}

blocks.code:
def crownGraph (α : Type*) : SimpleGraph (α ⊕ α) :=
  completeBipartiteGraph α α \ fromRel fun a b => ∃ i, a = Sum.inl i ∧ b = Sum.inr i
blocks.docstring:
The *crown graph* on the vertex type `α ⊕ α`: the complete bipartite graph
`completeBipartiteGraph α α` with the perfect matching `{Sum.inl i, Sum.inr i}` removed. For
`α = Fin m` this is the crown graph $H_{m,m}$ on $2m$ vertices.

justification.closest_existing_considered: Mathlib's `completeBipartiteGraph` (used as the base); Mathlib has no crown graph.
justification.name: BipartiteGraph.crownGraph
justification.why_needed: The crown graph H_{m,m} = K_{m,m} minus a perfect matching, defined literally as `completeBipartiteGraph α α \ fromRel (matching {inl i, inr i})` on `α ⊕ α`; `crownGraph (Fin m)` is H_{m,m}. API lemmas give its adjacency (`inl i ~ inr j ↔ i ≠ j`, no edges within a side), bipartiteness, and H_{1,1} = ⊥.

blocks.code:
@[category API, AMS 5 68]
theorem representationNumber_top (n : ℕ) :
    representationNumber (⊤ : SimpleGraph (Fin (n + 1))) = 1 := by
  have h1 : IsKRepresentable (⊤ : SimpleGraph (Fin (n + 1))) 1 := by
    refine ⟨List.finRange (n + 1), ⟨fun v => List.mem_finRange v, fun x y hxy => ?_⟩,
      fun v => List.count_eq_one_of_mem (List.nodup_finRange _) (List.mem_finRange v)⟩
    simpa [hxy, Alternate] using ((List.nodup_finRange (n + 1)).filter _).isChain
  refine le_antisymm (Nat.sInf_le h1) (Nat.one_le_iff_ne_zero.2 fun h0 => ?_)
  obtain ⟨w, ⟨hw, -⟩, hcount⟩ :=
    (Nat.sInf_eq_zero.1 h0).resolve_right (Set.Nonempty.ne_empty ⟨1, h1⟩)
  exact absurd (hcount 0) (List.count_pos_iff.2 (hw 0)).ne'
blocks.docstring:
A non-empty complete graph has representation number `1`: it is represented by a permutation
of its vertices, and no graph with a vertex is represented by a word with `0` copies of each
letter.

@[category API, AMS 5 68]
theorem eq_top_of_isKRepresentable_one (G : SimpleGraph V) (h : IsKRepresentable G 1) :
    G = ⊤ := by
  obtain ⟨w, ⟨-, h⟩, hw⟩ := h
  have hnd : w.Nodup := List.nodup_iff_count_le_one.mpr fun v => (hw v).le
  ext x y
  exact ⟨fun h => h.ne, fun hxy => (h x y hxy).mp (hnd.filter _).isChain⟩
blocks.docstring:
A `1`-uniform word is a permutation of the vertices, and a permutation represents the
complete graph: the only `1`-representable graphs are the complete graphs.

@[category test, AMS 5 68]
theorem representationNumber_crownGraph_two :
    representationNumber (crownGraph (Fin 2)) = 2 := by
  refine le_antisymm (Nat.sInf_le isKRepresentable_crownGraph_two_two)
    (le_csInf ⟨2, isKRepresentable_crownGraph_two_two⟩ ?_)
  rintro (_ | _ | k) hk
  · exact (not_isKRepresentable_zero _ hk).elim
  · have := congrArg (fun G => G.Adj (Sum.inl 0) (Sum.inr 0)) (eq_top_of_isKRepresentable_one _ hk)
    simp [crownGraph_adj_inl_inr] at this
  · omega

Is it true that out of all bipartite graphs, crown graphs require longest word-representants?

Precisely: is it true that for every $m$ and every bipartite graph $G$ on $2m$ vertices, the
representation number of $G$ is at most that of the crown graph $H_{m,m}$ on $2m$ vertices, i.e.
$\mathcal{R}(G) \le \mathcal{R}(H_{m,m})$? A graph on $n$ vertices represented with $k$ copies
of each letter is represented by a word of length $kn$, so this says that among the bipartite
graphs on a given number of vertices the crown graph needs the longest word-representants.
Crown graphs have an even number of vertices, so only even orders are compared; a bipartite
graph on $2m + 1$ vertices is an induced subgraph of one on $2m + 2$ vertices. No lower bound on
$m$ is imposed: the comparison is with $\mathcal{R}(H_{m,m})$ itself rather than with the formula
$\lceil m/2 \rceil$, which only holds for $m \ge 5$.

/--
Is it true that out of all bipartite graphs, crown graphs require longest word-representants?

Precisely: is it true that for every $m$ and every bipartite graph $G$ on $2m$ vertices, the
representation number of $G$ is at most that of the crown graph $H_{m,m}$ on $2m$ vertices, i.e.
$\mathcal{R}(G) \le \mathcal{R}(H_{m,m})$? A graph on $n$ vertices represented with $k$ copies
of each letter is represented by a word of length $kn$, so this says that among the bipartite
graphs on a given number of vertices the crown graph needs the longest word-representants.
Crown graphs have an even number of vertices, so only even orders are compared; a bipartite
graph on $2m + 1$ vertices is an induced subgraph of one on $2m + 2$ vertices. No lower bound on
$m$ is imposed: the comparison is with $\mathcal{R}(H_{m,m})$ itself rather than with the formula
$\lceil m/2 \rceil$, which only holds for $m \ge 5$.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 5 68]
theorem bipartite_graph :
    answer(sorry) ↔ ∀ (m : ℕ) (G : SimpleGraph (Fin (2 * m))), G.IsBipartite →
      representationNumber G ≤ representationNumber (crownGraph (Fin m)) := by
  sorry
end BipartiteGraph

claims.decomposer_note: Single yes/no question (Kitaev–Lozin / Glen–Kitaev–Pyatkin open problem): with R(G) the representation number (least k such that G is represented by a word containing exactly k copies of each letter; every bipartite graph is word-representable), it asks whether for every bipartite graph G on n vertices R(G) ≤ R of the crown graph H_{m,m} = K_{m,m} minus a perfect matching on the same number of vertices (= ⌈m/2⌉ = ⌈n/4⌉ when n = 2m ≥ 10); the comparison is implicitly among graphs with the same vertex count, and the treatment of odd n and small n (where R(H_{4,4}) = 3 breaks the ⌈m/2⌉ formula) is a convention the formalizer must fix, e.g. by comparing against crown graphs on at most n vertices or restricting to n ≥ n₀; the background article itself never mentions word-representants, so all definitions come from the cited word-representable-graph literature.
claims.reviewer_why: c08's statement `answer(sorry) ↔ ∀ m, ∀ bipartite G : SimpleGraph (Fin (2*m)), R(G) ≤ R(crownGraph (Fin m))` is the literal same-vertex-count reading with correct bespoke definitions (alternation via filter+IsChain(≠), representation requiring every letter to occur and Adj ↔ alternate for distinct letters, k-uniform words, sInf-based representation number, crown graph = K_{m,m} minus the matching {inl i, inr i}). I chose the unrestricted version (c01/c03/c07/c08) over the m ≥ 5 versions (c02/c04/c06) after independently brute-forcing the small cases: all bipartite graphs on ≤ 6 vertices are circle graphs (R ≤ 2 = R(H_{m,m}), m ≤ 3), every bipartite graph on 8 vertices other than H_{4,4} has an orientation of poset dimension ≤ 3 (so R ≤ 3), and Q_3 = H_{4,4} is not a circle graph (R ≥ 3); hence the unrestricted statement is equivalent to the m ≥ 5 one and more literal. Edits: fixed a loose docstring phrase ('shortest uniform word-representant'), added API/tests ported from c03 (not_isKRepresentable_zero, eq_top_of_isKRepresentable_one, R(H_{2,2}) = 2) and the Glen–Kitaev–Pyatkin `research solved` companion R(H_{m,m}) = ⌈m/2⌉ for m ≥ 5 (as in c01/c07), plus a docstring note that no lower bound on m is imposed.

context:
In the mathematical field of graph theory, a bipartite graph (or bigraph) is a graph whose vertices can be divided into two disjoint and independent sets $U$ and $V$, that is, every edge connects a vertex in $U$ to one in $V$. Vertex sets $U$ and $V$ are usually called the parts of the graph. Equivalently, a bipartite graph is a graph that does not contain any odd-length cycles.
The two sets $U$ and $V$ may be thought of as a coloring of the graph with two colors: if one colors all nodes in $U$ blue, and all nodes in $V$ red, each edge has endpoints of differing colors, as is required in the graph coloring problem. In contrast, such a coloring is impossible in the case of a non-bipartite graph, such as a triangle: after one node is colored blue and another red, the third vertex of the triangle is connected to vertices of both colors, preventing it from being assigned either color.
One often writes $G=(U,V,E)$ to denote a bipartite graph whose partition has the parts $U$ and $V$, with $E$ denoting the edges of the graph. If a bipartite graph is not connected, it may have more than one bipartition; in this case, the $(U,V,E)$ notation is helpful in specifying one particular bipartition that may be of importance in an application. import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Bipartite graphs: do crown graphs require the longest word-representants?

A graph $G = (V, E)$ is *word-representable* if there is a word $w$ over the alphabet $V$ (every
letter of $V$ occurring in $w$) such that two distinct letters $x, y$ *alternate* in $w$ if and
only if $xy \in E$. Here $x$ and $y$ alternate in $w$ if deleting from $w$ all letters other than
$x$ and $y$ leaves a word of the form $xyxy\cdots$ or $yxyx\cdots$ (of even or odd length). The
graph $G$ is *$k$-representable* if it is represented by a word containing exactly $k$ copies of
each letter; the least such $k$ is the *representation number* $\mathcal{R}(G)$. A word
representing a graph on $n$ vertices with $k$ copies of each letter has length $kn$, so
$\mathcal{R}(G)$ measures the length of the shortest uniform word-representant of $G$. Every
bipartite graph is word-representable.

The *crown graph* $H_{m,m}$ is obtained from the complete bipartite graph $K_{m,m}$ by removing a
perfect matching. Glen, Kitaev and Pyatkin proved that $\mathcal{R}(H_{m,m}) = \lceil m/2 \rceil$
for $m \ge 5$.

The open problem asks whether, among all bipartite graphs, the crown graphs require the longest
word-representants: is $\mathcal{R}(G) \le \mathcal{R}(H_{m,m})$ for every bipartite graph $G$
on $2m$ vertices?

*References:*
- [Wikipedia, Bipartite graph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/bipartite_graph)
- [Wikipedia, List of unsolved problems in mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_unsolved_problems_in_mathematics)
- S. Kitaev, *A comprehensive introduction to the theory of word-representable graphs*,
  [arXiv:1705.05924](https://arxiv.org/abs/1705.05924)
- M. Glen, S. Kitaev, A. Pyatkin, *On the representation number of a crown graph*,
  Discrete Applied Mathematics 244 (2018), 89–93,
  [arXiv:1609.00674](https://arxiv.org/abs/1609.00674)
- S. Kitaev, V. Lozin, *Words and Graphs*, Monographs in Theoretical Computer Science,
  Springer (2015)
-/

namespace BipartiteGraph

open SimpleGraph

variable {V : Type*} [DecidableEq V]

/-- Two letters `x` and `y` *alternate* in the word `w` if deleting from `w` all letters other
than `x` and `y` leaves a word with no two consecutive equal letters, i.e. a word of the form
`xyxy…` or `yxyx…` (of even or odd length). -/
def Alternate (w : List V) (x y : V) : Prop :=
  (w.filter fun z => z = x ∨ z = y).IsChain (· ≠ ·)

/-- A word `w` over the alphabet `V` *represents* the graph `G` if every letter of `V` occurs in
`w`, and two distinct letters alternate in `w` if and only if they are adjacent in `G`. -/
def IsRepresentedBy (G : SimpleGraph V) (w : List V) : Prop :=
  (∀ v, v ∈ w) ∧ ∀ x y, x ≠ y → (Alternate w x y ↔ G.Adj x y)

/-- The graph `G` is *`k`-representable* if it is represented by a word containing exactly `k`
copies of each letter. -/
def IsKRepresentable (G : SimpleGraph V) (k : ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∃ w : List V, IsRepresentedBy G w ∧ ∀ v, w.count v = k

/-- The *representation number* $\mathcal{R}(G)$ of `G`: the least `k` such that `G` is
`k`-representable. By the `sInf` convention it is `0` when `G` is not word-representable; this
does not occur for bipartite graphs, which are all word-representable. -/
noncomputable def representationNumber (G : SimpleGraph V) : ℕ :=
  sInf {k | IsKRepresentable G k}

/-- The *crown graph* on the vertex type `α ⊕ α`: the complete bipartite graph
`completeBipartiteGraph α α` with the perfect matching `{Sum.inl i, Sum.inr i}` removed. For
`α = Fin m` this is the crown graph $H_{m,m}$ on $2m$ vertices. -/
def crownGraph (α : Type*) : SimpleGraph (α ⊕ α) :=
  completeBipartiteGraph α α \ fromRel fun a b => ∃ i, a = Sum.inl i ∧ b = Sum.inr i

@[category API, AMS 5]
theorem crownGraph_adj_inl_inr {α : Type*} (i j : α) :
    (crownGraph α).Adj (Sum.inl i) (Sum.inr j) ↔ i ≠ j := by
  simp [crownGraph, fromRel_adj, eq_comm]

@[category API, AMS 5]
theorem crownGraph_adj_inr_inl {α : Type*} (i j : α) :
    (crownGraph α).Adj (Sum.inr i) (Sum.inl j) ↔ i ≠ j := by
  rw [adj_comm, crownGraph_adj_inl_inr, ne_comm]

@[category API, AMS 5]
theorem crownGraph_adj_inl_inl {α : Type*} (i j : α) :
    ¬ (crownGraph α).Adj (Sum.inl i) (Sum.inl j) := by
  simp [crownGraph]

@[category API, AMS 5]
theorem crownGraph_adj_inr_inr {α : Type*} (i j : α) :
    ¬ (crownGraph α).Adj (Sum.inr i) (Sum.inr j) := by
  simp [crownGraph]

@[category API, AMS 5]
theorem crownGraph_isBipartite (α : Type*) : (crownGraph α).IsBipartite :=
  Colorable.mono_left sdiff_le (CompleteBipartiteGraph.bicoloring α α).colorable

/-- The crown graph $H_{1,1}$ has two vertices and no edges. -/
@[category test, AMS 5]
theorem crownGraph_fin_one : crownGraph (Fin 1) = ⊥ := by
  ext (i | i) (j | j) <;>
    simp [crownGraph_adj_inl_inr, crownGraph_adj_inr_inl, Fin.fin_one_eq_zero]

/-- The letters `0` and `1` alternate in the word `0101`. -/
@[category test, AMS 5 68]
theorem alternate_example : Alternate [0, 1, 0, 1] (0 : Fin 2) 1 := by
  unfold Alternate
  decide

/-- The letters `0` and `1` do not alternate in the word `0011`. -/
@[category test, AMS 5 68]
theorem not_alternate_example : ¬ Alternate [0, 0, 1, 1] (0 : Fin 2) 1 := by
  unfold Alternate
  decide

/-- The complete graph on three vertices is represented by the word `012`. -/
@[category test, AMS 5 68]
theorem isKRepresentable_top_one : IsKRepresentable (⊤ : SimpleGraph (Fin 3)) 1 :=
  ⟨[0, 1, 2], ⟨by decide, by unfold Alternate; decide⟩, by decide⟩

/-- The crown graph $H_{1,1}$ (two isolated vertices $a, b$) is represented by the word `aabb`. -/
@[category test, AMS 5 68]
theorem isKRepresentable_crownGraph_one_two : IsKRepresentable (crownGraph (Fin 1)) 2 := by
  refine ⟨[Sum.inl 0, Sum.inl 0, Sum.inr 0, Sum.inr 0], ⟨?_, ?_⟩, ?_⟩
  · rintro (i | i) <;> fin_cases i <;> simp
  · rintro (i | i) (j | j) <;> fin_cases i <;> fin_cases j <;>
      simp [Alternate, crownGraph_fin_one]
  · rintro (i | i) <;> fin_cases i <;> simp

/-- A non-empty complete graph has representation number `1`: it is represented by a permutation
of its vertices, and no graph with a vertex is represented by a word with `0` copies of each
letter. -/
@[category API, AMS 5 68]
theorem representationNumber_top (n : ℕ) :
    representationNumber (⊤ : SimpleGraph (Fin (n + 1))) = 1 := by
  have h1 : IsKRepresentable (⊤ : SimpleGraph (Fin (n + 1))) 1 := by
    refine ⟨List.finRange (n + 1), ⟨fun v => List.mem_finRange v, fun x y hxy => ?_⟩,
      fun v => List.count_eq_one_of_mem (List.nodup_finRange _) (List.mem_finRange v)⟩
    simpa [hxy, Alternate] using ((List.nodup_finRange (n + 1)).filter _).isChain
  refine le_antisymm (Nat.sInf_le h1) (Nat.one_le_iff_ne_zero.2 fun h0 => ?_)
  obtain ⟨w, ⟨hw, -⟩, hcount⟩ :=
    (Nat.sInf_eq_zero.1 h0).resolve_right (Set.Nonempty.ne_empty ⟨1, h1⟩)
  exact absurd (hcount 0) (List.count_pos_iff.2 (hw 0)).ne'

/-- A graph with at least one vertex is not `0`-representable, since a representing word must
contain every vertex. -/
@[category API, AMS 5 68]
theorem not_isKRepresentable_zero [Nonempty V] (G : SimpleGraph V) : ¬ IsKRepresentable G 0 := by
  rintro ⟨w, ⟨hmem, -⟩, hw⟩
  obtain ⟨v⟩ := ‹Nonempty V›
  exact (List.count_pos_iff.mpr (hmem v)).ne' (hw v)

/-- A `1`-uniform word is a permutation of the vertices, and a permutation represents the
complete graph: the only `1`-representable graphs are the complete graphs. -/
@[category API, AMS 5 68]
theorem eq_top_of_isKRepresentable_one (G : SimpleGraph V) (h : IsKRepresentable G 1) :
    G = ⊤ := by
  obtain ⟨w, ⟨-, h⟩, hw⟩ := h
  have hnd : w.Nodup := List.nodup_iff_count_le_one.mpr fun v => (hw v).le
  ext x y
  exact ⟨fun h => h.ne, fun hxy => (h x y hxy).mp (hnd.filter _).isChain⟩

/-- The crown graph $H_{2,2}$ (two disjoint edges $a b'$ and $b a'$) is `2`-representable, e.g. by
the word $a b' a b' a' b a' b$, where $a, b$ are the left and $a', b'$ the right vertices. -/
@[category test, AMS 5 68]
theorem isKRepresentable_crownGraph_two_two : IsKRepresentable (crownGraph (Fin 2)) 2 := by
  refine ⟨[.inl 0, .inr 1, .inl 0, .inr 1, .inr 0, .inl 1, .inr 0, .inl 1], ⟨?_, ?_⟩, ?_⟩
  · rintro (i | i) <;> fin_cases i <;> simp
  · rintro (i | i) (j | j) <;> fin_cases i <;> fin_cases j <;>
      simp [Alternate, crownGraph_adj_inl_inr, crownGraph_adj_inr_inl, crownGraph_adj_inl_inl,
        crownGraph_adj_inr_inr]
  · rintro (i | i) <;> fin_cases i <;> simp

/-- The representation number of the crown graph $H_{2,2}$ is `2`. -/
@[category test, AMS 5 68]
theorem representationNumber_crownGraph_two :
    representationNumber (crownGraph (Fin 2)) = 2 := by
  refine le_antisymm (Nat.sInf_le isKRepresentable_crownGraph_two_two)
    (le_csInf ⟨2, isKRepresentable_crownGraph_two_two⟩ ?_)
  rintro (_ | _ | k) hk
  · exact (not_isKRepresentable_zero _ hk).elim
  · have := congrArg (fun G => G.Adj (Sum.inl 0) (Sum.inr 0)) (eq_top_of_isKRepresentable_one _ hk)
    simp [crownGraph_adj_inl_inr] at this
  · omega

/--
**Glen–Kitaev–Pyatkin (2018).** For $m \ge 5$ the crown graph $H_{m,m}$ has representation
number $\lceil m/2 \rceil$. (The restriction $m \ge 5$ is needed: $H_{4,4}$ is the $3$-cube,
whose representation number is $3$.)
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 5 68]
theorem representationNumber_crownGraph (m : ℕ) (hm : 5 ≤ m) :
    representationNumber (crownGraph (Fin m)) = (m + 1) / 2 := by
  sorry

/--
Is it true that out of all bipartite graphs, crown graphs require longest word-representants?

Precisely: is it true that for every $m$ and every bipartite graph $G$ on $2m$ vertices, the
representation number of $G$ is at most that of the crown graph $H_{m,m}$ on $2m$ vertices, i.e.
$\mathcal{R}(G) \le \mathcal{R}(H_{m,m})$? A graph on $n$ vertices represented with $k$ copies
of each letter is represented by a word of length $kn$, so this says that among the bipartite
graphs on a given number of vertices the crown graph needs the longest word-representants.
Crown graphs have an even number of vertices, so only even orders are compared; a bipartite
graph on $2m + 1$ vertices is an induced subgraph of one on $2m + 2$ vertices. No lower bound on
$m$ is imposed: the comparison is with $\mathcal{R}(H_{m,m})$ itself rather than with the formula
$\lceil m/2 \rceil$, which only holds for $m \ge 5$.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 5 68]
theorem bipartite_graph :
    answer(sorry) ↔ ∀ (m : ℕ) (G : SimpleGraph (Fin (2 * m))), G.IsBipartite →
      representationNumber G ≤ representationNumber (crownGraph (Fin m)) := by
  sorry

end BipartiteGraph

items: 'Longest word-representants' is read via the representation number R(G) (least k with a representing word having exactly k copies of each letter), as the decomposition notes prescribe and as in Kitaev's survey / Glen–Kitaev–Pyatkin; a word with k copies of each of n letters has length kn, so for graphs with the same vertex count this is the same as comparing word lengths. An alternative reading (minimum length of a representing word with arbitrary letter multiplicities) is not the invariant used in the literature and was not formalized.

Comparison is among graphs with the same number of vertices: for every m, every bipartite graph on 2m vertices (modelled WLOG as `SimpleGraph (Fin (2*m))`) is compared with H_{m,m} = `crownGraph (Fin m)` on `Fin m ⊕ Fin m` (also 2m vertices). Only even orders are compared because crown graphs have even order; a bipartite graph on 2m+1 vertices is an induced subgraph of one on 2m+2 vertices, so the even-order statement implies the natural odd-order version.

No lower threshold on m was imposed (the statement in the source has none). I compare against R(H_{m,m}) itself rather than the formula ⌈m/2⌉, so the irregularity R(H_{4,4}) = 3 does not arise. Small cases do not make the statement trivially false: m = 0 is trivial (both sides 0); for m = 1, 2, 3 all bipartite graphs on ≤ 6 vertices are circle graphs (R ≤ 2 = R(H_{m,m})); for m = 4 every height-2 poset on 8 elements other than the standard example S_4 has dimension ≤ 3 (Hiraguchi/Bogart–Trotter–Kimble), giving R ≤ 3 = R(H_{4,4}). A reviewer may wish to double-check these small cases or add `5 ≤ m` if preferred.

`representationNumber` uses `sInf`, so it is 0 if the graph is not word-representable; this cannot happen for bipartite graphs (all bipartite graphs are comparability graphs, hence word-representable), so the inequality is never trivially satisfied for that reason. Words must contain every letter (`∀ v, v ∈ w`), matching the literature's convention that the word is over the alphabet V; this gives R(complete graph) = 1 (proved as `representationNumber_top`) rather than 0.
Bipartiteness is Mathlib's `SimpleGraph.IsBipartite` (= `Colorable 2`), which includes edgeless graphs and graphs with isolated vertices, matching the informal 'all bipartite graphs'.

Definitions require `[DecidableEq V]` (for `List.filter` and `List.count`); the `BEq` used by `List.count` is the one derived from `DecidableEq`, so it is lawful for all vertex types including `Fin m ⊕ Fin m`.

The problem is posed as a yes/no question, so it is stated as `answer(sorry) ↔ …`; `answer(True)` asserts crown graphs are extremal, `answer(False)` asserts some bipartite graph on 2m vertices has a larger representation number than H_{m,m}.

reviewer_notes: Ambiguities in the source: the list entry gives no vertex count; all candidates and the decomposition agree the comparison is among graphs with the same number of vertices (otherwise the question is vacuous since R(H_{m,m}) → ∞). Crown graphs have even order, so the statement quantifies over bipartite graphs on 2m vertices; the odd case follows from monotonicity of R under induced subgraphs (add an isolated vertex). 'Longest word-representants' is read as the representation number (least k with a k-uniform representant), the invariant used by Kitaev–Lozin / Glen–Kitaev–Pyatkin. Candidate conventions: c02/c04/c06 restricted to m ≥ 5 — acceptable but weaker than necessary; c05 compared bipartite graphs on any n ≥ 10 vertices (odd too) with H_{⌊n/2⌋,⌊n/2⌋}, which strengthens the question beyond the source (and the analogous claim fails at n = 7 via Q_3 minus a vertex), so it was not used. I verified by brute force (C++) that the unrestricted even-order statement holds for m ≤ 4, so shipping without a lower bound does not make the answer trivially determined. The final file is c08's declaration with docstring edits and extra API/test lemmas from c03, plus the GKP research-solved theorem. Compiled with `lake env lean --json`: only two `declaration uses 'sorry'` warnings (the research solved GKP theorem and the open problem). One module-docstring line exceeds 100 chars only because of an unbreakable Wikipedia URL, as in other repository files.
